bundleEnforcement.description:
Enterprise Rego/OPA policy bundles
Bundle enforcement mode: `optional` or `required`. The server requires a
valid value here and refuses to start without one, so the chart always
renders it. `optional` evaluates whatever `bundles` lists and falls back to
YAML-only trust-policy authorization when the list is empty. `required` turns
the Rego layer into a startup precondition: at least one bundle must be
configured, every entry needs an `expected_policy_revision` and an `oci://`
ref pinned to `
`cosign.skip_verification` must stay false, and a bundle that applies to
every app (`apps: []`) must use `fail_mode: closed`.

`registry.auth.password_file`, or `cosign.public_key_ref`, mount the file
with `extraVolumes` and `extraVolumeMounts` and point the field at the
mounted path.

endpointAuth.description:
Bearer tokens for the operational endpoints. Both are optional and empty by
default, which leaves the endpoints unauthenticated. The broker treats an
empty token as "no auth required".

Tokens are never written into the ConfigMap. The chart puts them in a Secret
and injects them as GITHUBSTS_HEALTH_AUTH_TOKEN and
GITHUBSTS_METRICS_AUTH_TOKEN, which the broker reads in preference to the
config file. The health token is also inlined into the liveness probe's pod
spec because the kubelet cannot resolve a Secret reference for HTTP headers.

existingSecret.description:
Existing Secret holding the tokens. When empty and a token is set below,
the chart creates a Secret of its own. Point this at your own Secret when
the token comes from an external secret manager. The chart then renders no
Secret and only references it, and the two key names below declare which
tokens that Secret actually holds.

metricsKey.description:
Key inside the Secret holding the /metrics bearer token. Clear it to
declare that `existingSecret` holds no metrics token. The chart then wires

otherwise point Prometheus at a key that does not exist and break the
scrape.

metricsToken.description:
Bearer token required on `GET /metrics`. Empty leaves /metrics open.
Prometheus needs the same token. See
`serviceMonitor.bearerTokenSecret`. Ignored when `existingSecret` is set.
metricsToken.title: metricsToken

github.description:
GitHub App configuration (required)
Each entry under apps is a logical app identified by name.
The app name is used in policy paths: {policy.basePath}/{appName}/{identity}.sts.yaml
Every private key must be stored in an existing Kubernetes Secret.
For a single-app deployment, define one entry (e.g. "default").

An entry is backed either by one GitHub App (`appId` + `existingSecret`) or by
a pool of several under `instances`, which spreads exchanges for that app name
across independent GitHub rate-limit buckets. The two forms are mutually
exclusive on one entry; the chart fails the render if both are set.

Pooled apps require a github-sts image that knows `instances:`, meaning 0.1.1
or later, which is what this chart's `appVersion` pins. An older image rejects
the key outright instead of falling back to the flat form. The config decoder
runs with known-fields checking, so the pod CrashLoopBackOffs with
`field instances not found in type config.AppConfig`. Only an `image.tag` or
`image.digest` override below the `appVersion` reaches that state.

`policyResolution` decides which repository wins when both the requesting repo
and the organization policy repo hold a policy for an identity. It only means
anything alongside `orgPolicyRepo`, and the server defaults it to `org_first`
whenever one is set.

requireImmutableSubjectClaims.description:
Require GitHub.com Actions tokens to carry immutable owner and
repository IDs inside the `sub` claim, in the form
`repo:OWNER
broker's own default, so rendering it changes nothing until you set it
to false.

It gates only what `sub` must contain. The separate signed
`repository_id` and `repository_owner_id` claims are mandatory for every
GitHub.com token either way, and the broker cross-checks them against
the subject before audience, replay or policy work. Tokens from any
other issuer are unaffected, and the immutable format does not exist on
GitHub Enterprise Server.

Repositories created before 2026-07-15 keep the name-only subject format
until they opt in through the organization or repository Actions OIDC
setting, or the REST API. Until a repository has opted in, its exchanges
are rejected with
`githubsts_oidc_validation_errors_total{reason="github_identity_immutable_subject_required"}`.

Set false only as an explicit, temporary migration posture: the legacy
name-only subject is vulnerable to repository namespace reuse, so an
attacker who acquires an abandoned owner/repo name can present a subject
that matches a trust policy written for the original. The broker logs a
startup warning, reports
`security.require_immutable_subject_claims: false` on `/health`, and
drops the `githubsts_oidc_immutable_subject_claims_required` gauge to 0
so the posture is alertable.
requireImmutableSubjectClaims.title: requireImmutableSubjectClaims

requiredAudience.description:
Server-wide required `aud` claim. When set, every token must carry
this value before any policy lookup or JTI reservation runs — defense
in depth on top of the per-policy `audience:` field. Leave empty to
rely solely on per-policy `audience:` enforcement. Recommended in
production: set this to the public URL of your STS deployment so a
misconfigured or permissive policy file cannot accept tokens minted
for an unrelated relying party.
requiredAudience.title: requiredAudience

trustedJwksHosts.description:
Per-issuer JWKS host overrides. Default behavior pins the JWKS
`Host` header to the issuer host (so a malicious DNS answer for the
issuer cannot redirect signing-key fetches elsewhere). This map is the
escape hatch for issuers that legitimately publish JWKS on a different
host — Google's `accounts.google.com` issues tokens but serves JWKS
from `www.googleapis.com`, for example. Keys are full issuer URLs
(with scheme), values are lists of allowed hostnames.

Verify before pinning:
  curl -s https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration \
    | jq -r .jwks_uri

When `networkPolicy.cilium.enabled=true`, hosts in this map are
auto-appended to the FQDN egress allow-list alongside issuer hosts.
Native NetworkPolicy users must add the corresponding CIDRs to
`networkPolicy.native.cidrs` manually (no FQDN matching available).
trustedJwksHosts.title: trustedJwksHosts

mode.description:
Probe transport for the startup / readiness / liveness probes.
`auto` (default) picks `httpGet` over HTTP, `httpGet` over HTTPS when
`tls.enabled`, and `tcpSocket` when `tls.clientAuth.enabled` — the kubelet
cannot present a client certificate, so an HTTP probe against an mTLS
listener fails the handshake and would crash-loop the pod. Force a specific
transport with `httpGet` or `tcpSocket`; note that `tcpSocket` only proves
the listener accepts connections, not that `/ready` returns 200. Also use
`tcpSocket` with `endpointAuth.existingSecret`, because the kubelet cannot
read that Secret to construct the liveness Authorization header.

initialDelaySeconds.title: initialDelaySeconds

startup.description:
Startup probe configuration. While the startup probe is running, liveness
and readiness probes are suspended — this lets you grant a long startup
budget without weakening steady-state liveness sensitivity. Disabled by
default since the default image starts well under the liveness threshold;
enable when cold start (JWKS fetch, policy cache warm, restoring a large
JTI cache from Redis) can exceed `probes.liveness.initialDelaySeconds +
probes.liveness.periodSeconds * probes.liveness.failureThreshold`,
otherwise liveness would kill the pod before it ever becomes ready.

enabled.description:
Enable startup probe. When true, liveness/readiness are gated until
this probe first succeeds.

failureThreshold.description:
Number of consecutive failures before the kubelet gives up and
restarts the container. Maximum startup time =
`failureThreshold * periodSeconds` (default 30 * 5s = 150s).
failureThreshold.title: failureThreshold

initialDelaySeconds.description:
Seconds the kubelet waits after the container starts before the
first probe. Usually 0 since `failureThreshold * periodSeconds`
already provides the startup budget.
initialDelaySeconds.title: initialDelaySeconds

periodSeconds.description:
Seconds between probe attempts. Combined with `failureThreshold`
it sets the maximum allowed startup time.
periodSeconds.title: periodSeconds

timeoutSeconds.description:
Per-attempt HTTP timeout. Increase if startup work makes `/ready`
respond slowly under contention.
timeoutSeconds.title: timeoutSeconds

revisionHistoryLimit.description:
Maximum number of old ReplicaSets retained for `kubectl rollout undo`.
Each pod-template change (image bump, ConfigMap checksum change, values
tweak) produces a new ReplicaSet; the old ones stay scaled to 0 as history.
Higher = deeper rollback window but more etcd objects and `kubectl get rs`
noise; lower = leaner cluster state but fewer rollback targets. Set to 0 to
disable rollback entirely. The Kubernetes default is 10; 5 is a balance for
this chart since `checksum/config` causes a roll on every config change.

Render the `helm test` hook pods. Automatically skipped when
`tls.clientAuth.enabled` is true, since the probe pods have no client
certificate to present and every request would be rejected at the
handshake.

Image the test pods run. The test script uses `curl` when the image
provides it and falls back to `wget`, so a curl image can be dropped in as

tls.description:
Native TLS / mTLS served by github-sts itself. This is deliberately separate
from `ingress.tls`, which terminates TLS at the ingress controller and then
forwards plain HTTP to the pod. Enable this block when the hop between the
proxy and the pod must also be encrypted (Gateway API `BackendTLSPolicy`, a
re-encrypting service mesh, PCI/FedRAMP-style "encryption in transit
everywhere" rules), when nothing fronts the Service at all, or when clients
must authenticate with a certificate (mTLS).

Requires a github-sts image that understands the `server.tls` config section.
Older images ignore it silently and keep serving plain HTTP, which then fails
the HTTPS probes this block turns on — check the app version before enabling.

certKey.description: Key inside `existingSecret` holding the PEM certificate chain.

cipherSuites.description:
TLS 1.2 cipher suite allow-list, as IANA names
(e.g. `TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256`). Empty means the Go
defaults: ECDHE key exchange throughout, AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305
preferred, but AES-CBC with a SHA-1 MAC still accepted. Pin the list when
that last part is not acceptable. Must be empty when `minVersion` is
`"1.3"`, where suites are not configurable and the application rejects the
combination at startup.
cipherSuites.title: cipherSuites

clientAuth.description: Mutual TLS: require and verify a client certificate on every connection.

in `clientAuth.caKey`. Verification is enforced for the whole listener — `/health`,
`/ready` and `/metrics` included — so the chart switches the kubelet
probes to `tcpSocket` (the kubelet cannot present a client certificate)
and skips the `helm test` hooks. Prometheus needs client credentials in
`serviceMonitor.tlsConfig` / `podMonitor.tlsConfig` to keep scraping.

existingSecret.description:
Existing Secret holding the trusted client CA bundle. Defaults to
`tls.existingSecret`, which is convenient when cert-manager writes
`ca.crt` alongside the serving cert. Point it at a separate Secret when
the client CA is a different trust root than the serving CA.

Serve HTTPS directly from the pod. Switches the container port name to
`https`, points the probes at the HTTPS scheme, and makes the chart mount
`existingSecret` into the pod. Terminating at the ingress/Gateway remains
the simpler model; reach for this only when the extra hop matters.

existingSecret.description:
Existing Secret holding the server certificate and private key. Required
when `tls.enabled` is true. A standard `kubernetes.io/tls` Secret works as
is (cert-manager, an internal PKI, or `kubectl create secret tls`); an
Opaque Secret works too as long as `certKey` / `keyKey` name its keys. The
chart never generates certificates — a self-signed cert is a local-testing
tool, not a deployment target.
existingSecret.title: existingSecret

keyKey.description: Key inside `existingSecret` holding the PEM private key.
keyKey.title: keyKey

minVersion.description:
Minimum accepted TLS version: `"1.2"` or `"1.3"`. Raise to `"1.3"` when
every client supports it: the suites stop being configurable and the
TLS 1.2 negotiation surface goes away, at the cost of rejecting older
clients outright.
minVersion.title: minVersion

mountPath.description:
Directory the certificate material is mounted at. A directory of its
own by default, which keeps it out of `/etc/github-sts`, where the config
ConfigMap and the per-app key mounts already live. Any path the container
does not already use works.
mountPath.title: mountPath

- TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
- TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256

Empty or `"0"` disables it. Kubernetes updates a mounted Secret in place on
renewal, so without polling a cert-manager rotation only takes effect at
the next pod restart. Set this to something well under the renewal window
(cert-manager renews at 2/3 of lifetime by default) for rotation without a
rollout.
reloadInterval.title: reloadInterval

tls.title: tls

tracing.description:
Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry). Off by default.

Spans need github-sts 0.1.2 or later, which is what this chart's `appVersion`
pins. 0.1.1 accepts the same settings and starts the exporter, but emits no
spans.

An image predating the `tracing:` config key rejects it outright — the server
decodes its config with KnownFields(true) — but the chart omits the whole
section when `enabled` is false, so a pinned older `image.tag` stays safe.

What the server emits: one root server span per request, by the
handler that sits outermost in the middleware chain. The span is named by
route — "POST /sts/exchange", never the raw path, because a path carries
repository names and would make span names unbounded — and carries
`http.route` plus roughly thirty `sts.*` and `github.*` attributes: app and
instance, scope, identity, result, OIDC issuer and subject, source and target
repository, the four-set permission chain, policy provenance, the bundle
decision, client address and user agent. They are built from the same audit
event as the audit line, at the one point every exit path of the handler
funnels through, so a span and its audit record cannot drift apart.

Each stage of an exchange is a child of that root span, so a slow exchange
shows where the time went: `sts.oidc.validate`, `sts.jti.reserve`,
`github.target.resolve`, `sts.policy.load`, `sts.policy.evaluate`,
`sts.bundle.evaluate` and `sts.token.issue`, among others. GitHub work nests
below them (`github.app_pool.attempt`, then `github.token.mint`), and the
outbound requests to GitHub, OIDC discovery and JWKS carry OpenTelemetry HTTP
client spans. A stage that never ran, because an earlier one rejected the
request, has no span.

A policy denial leaves the span status Unset rather than Error — a denial is
a working broker doing its job, and marking it Error would make span-derived
error rates track how often the trust policy fired. The outcome lives in the
`sts.result` attribute instead. Error is reserved for a cache fault, an
upstream GitHub error, and the bundle conditions that fail closed with a 503.

Probe and scrape paths (/health, /ready, /healthz, /readyz, /metrics) are
filtered and produce no spans, so a one-second kubelet probe cannot outnumber
real exchanges in the backend. An inbound traceparent is honoured rather than
replaced, so an exchange joins the calling workflow's trace.

Note that `trace_id` is 32 hex characters from v0.1.1 onward whether or not
this is enabled; the widening came with the image, not with this setting.

Two lines turn export on:
  tracing.enabled=true
  tracing.endpoint=otel-collector.observability:4317

Traces are sampled diagnostics, not an audit trail: the audit log stays the
system of record for authorization decisions.

enabled.description:
Export OTLP traces to `tracing.endpoint`. When false the server installs
a no-op tracer, so instrumentation costs effectively nothing.
enabled.title: enabled

endpoint.description:
Collector address as bare `host:port` — no scheme. The server passes
this to the OTLP exporter's `WithEndpoint`, which does not parse URLs, so
`http://collector:4317` fails at export time rather than at startup; the
chart rejects it during rendering instead. The protocol default port
(4317 for grpc, 4318 for http) is appended when you omit one. Use
`localhost:4317` for a collector running as a sidecar. Required when
`tracing.enabled` is true. An IPv6 literal must carry its own brackets and
port, e.g. `[::1]:4317`.
endpoint.title: endpoint

environment.description:
`deployment.environment` resource attribute (e.g. `staging`, `prod`).
Omitted from the config when empty.
environment.title: environment

headersSecret.description:
Authentication headers for a collector that requires them. These are
credentials, so the chart passes them through the environment as
`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` instead of rendering them into the ConfigMap,
which is readable by anyone holding `get configmaps` in the namespace. The
server leaves its own `headers` field unset, which is what lets the
standard OTEL variable take effect.

key.description:
Key inside `headersSecret.name`. The value uses OTLP header syntax:
comma-separated `key=value` pairs, e.g. `api-key=abc,x-tenant=acme`.
key.title: key

name.description:
Existing Secret holding the header string. Empty disables the
environment variable entirely.
name.title: name

headersSecret.title: headersSecret

insecure.description:
Export over plaintext. Defaults to true because the deployment this is
built for is a hop to an in-cluster collector on the pod network, where
there is no certificate to verify and TLS would only fail the handshake.
Set to false when exporting straight to a vendor endpoint over the
internet, and pair it with `tracing.headersSecret` for the API key.
insecure.title: insecure

sampleRatio.description:
Head sampling ratio between 0 and 1, applied `ParentBased` so an
inbound sampling decision is respected. Keep this at 1.0 and tail-sample in
the Collector instead: the exchange result is not known when a head sampler
runs, so sampling down here throws away denials and failovers at random —
exactly the traces worth keeping for a security broker.
sampleRatio.title: sampleRatio

serviceName.description:
`service.name` resource attribute. Empty uses the server's own default,
`github-sts`. Override it when two releases export to the same tracing
backend and need to be told apart; leaving it alone keeps the value that
shipped dashboards and alerts key on.
serviceName.title: serviceName

timeout.description:
Per-export timeout (Go duration string). Note that this always wins over
`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT`, which the server never consults.
timeout.title: timeout

tracing.title: tracing
